# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Biotechnology is a Semester 6 subject carrying 4 theory credits. It bridges the molecular biology you studied in earlier years with the practical reality of how modern protein drugs are made, tested and regulated. The subject is unusually broad — it touches virology, microbiology, immunology, process engineering, analytical chemistry and pharmacoeconomics — but the exam rewards students who can explain a few key processes clearly and completely, with labelled diagrams.

**Prerequisites.** A solid grasp of Microbiology and Immunology (earlier semesters) is assumed throughout. If the terms "antibody", "antigen", "gram-positive", "plasmid", "promoter" and "restriction enzyme" are unfamiliar, revisit those notes first.

**How the units here match the syllabus.** The PCI syllabus has five units, and these notes keep one file per unit in the same order. Unit 1 covers the molecular tools; Unit 2 covers how those tools are used to make specific proteins; Unit 3 covers antibodies, vaccines and diagnostics; Unit 4 covers fermentation; Unit 5 covers purification and regulation.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, as universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; learn the full answer, include a labelled diagram where relevant.
- **Medium** — asked every few years, or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for the objective section and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in pharmacy papers, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Recombinant DNA Technology | Steps in gene cloning (restriction digestion, ligation, transformation, selection), PCR (components, cycle, applications), Sanger dideoxy sequencing, types of vectors (plasmid/BAC/YAC), Southern/Northern/Western blotting, restriction endonucleases — types I/II/III |
| 2 Expression Systems and Recombinant Proteins | *E. coli* vs mammalian expression (inclusion bodies, glycosylation), recombinant insulin production (proinsulin route in *E. coli*/yeast), recombinant EPO (why CHO cells, uses), G-CSF and GM-CSF, interferons (types, uses, SE), coagulation factors for haemophilia |
| 3 Monoclonal Antibodies, Vaccines, Diagnostics | Hybridoma technology (all steps, HAT selection), chimeric vs humanised vs fully human mAbs, ELISA (sandwich, indirect, competitive), recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (yeast), DNA vaccines, viral vector vaccines, lateral flow immunoassays |
| 4 Fermentation Technology | Batch vs fed-batch vs continuous fermentation, bioreactor components (draw and label), penicillin fermentation (*P. chrysogenum*, fed-batch, precursor feeding, non-growth-associated kinetics), upstream processing (medium, inoculum, sterilisation), scale-up criteria |
| 5 Downstream Processing | DSP four stages, Protein A chromatography for mAbs, cell disruption methods, viral clearance (orthogonal steps, ICH Q5A), lyophilisation steps and excipients, LAL test, biosimilar vs originator, BLA (FDA) / EMA / CDSCO regulatory pathways |

**High-probability topics (most likely to appear in Section B or as a 5-mark question):**

1. Steps in gene cloning with a flow diagram
2. PCR — components, cycle and applications
3. Hybridoma technology — step by step
4. Recombinant insulin — history and production
5. Recombinant EPO — why mammalian cells, uses and misuse
6. ELISA — sandwich ELISA mechanism and applications
7. Penicillin fermentation — organism, process, kinetics
8. Downstream processing of a monoclonal antibody
9. Biosimilar vs biologic originator
10. Viral clearance strategies in biopharmaceutical manufacture

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Draw labelled diagrams.** Examiners in this subject award marks for diagrams that most other pharmacy subjects do not test: draw the bioreactor (impeller, sparger, baffles, pH/DO probes, jacket), the hybridoma technology flowchart, and the gene cloning scheme. Even a rough diagram with correct labels scores marks.
2. **For MCQs, know the enzyme names and their actions.** Restriction enzyme names (EcoRI, HindIII), Taq polymerase (heat-stable, 72°C), T4 DNA ligase (seals nicks), Protein A (binds Fc of IgG) and Limulus amebocyte lysate (endotoxin test) appear repeatedly.
3. **Classify and name before explaining.** When asked about expression systems, give the name (*E. coli*, yeast, CHO), state the key advantage and limitation, then explain the detail. Examiners count correct examples.
4. **Distinguish the antibody naming suffixes.** -omab = murine; -ximab = chimeric; -zumab = humanised; -umab = fully human. Learn at least one example for each.
5. **Link the product to the host.** For any recombinant protein, state clearly which host is used and why. EPO → CHO (needs glycosylation); insulin → *E. coli* or yeast (small, no glycan needed); mAbs → CHO (Fc glycosylation needed for effector function).
6. **For regulatory questions, name all three agencies.** CDSCO (India), FDA (USA), EMA (Europe). Know the BLA pathway for the exam; Indian students are also asked about CDSCO.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, master these six: **gene cloning steps**, **PCR cycle**, **hybridoma technology**, **penicillin fermentation**, **mAb downstream processing**, and **biosimilar vs originator**. Then read the recombinant proteins table and the comparison tables once each.

## Key terms to know cold

| Term | One-line definition |
| --- | --- |
| Restriction endonuclease | Bacterial enzyme that cuts dsDNA at a specific palindromic sequence |
| DNA ligase (T4) | Seals nicks in dsDNA using ATP; joins sticky or blunt ends in cloning |
| Vector | DNA molecule (plasmid, phage, BAC, YAC) that carries a foreign gene into a host and allows replication |
| Competent cells | Bacteria made able to take up foreign DNA (CaCl₂ treatment or electroporation) |
| Sticky ends | Single-stranded overhangs produced by most Type II restriction enzymes; allow annealing with complementary ends |
| IPTG | Isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside; non-metabolisable inducer of *lac* promoter in *E. coli* |
| Inclusion bodies | Insoluble aggregates of recombinant protein in *E. coli*; require solubilisation and refolding |
| Hybridoma | Cell formed by fusing a B lymphocyte with a myeloma cell; immortal and antibody-secreting |
| HAT medium | Hypoxanthine, aminopterin, thymidine; selects only hybridomas (unfused myeloma cells die) |
| CDR | Complementarity-determining region; the antigen-contact loops within the variable domain |
| Biosimilar | Biologic approved on the basis of demonstrated similarity to an approved reference product |
| Lyophilisation | Freeze-drying; freezing followed by sublimation of ice under vacuum |
| LAL test | Limulus amebocyte lysate test; detects bacterial endotoxin |
| Protein A | *S. aureus* protein that binds Fc of IgG; used as the first capture step in mAb purification |
| Fed-batch | Fermentation mode in which nutrients are added during the run; extends productive phase |

## Comparison tables

### *E. coli* vs eukaryotic expression systems

| Feature | *E. coli* | Yeast (*Pichia*) | CHO cells |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Growth rate | Very fast (20 min doubling) | Fast | Slow (24 h doubling) |
| Cost | Very low | Low | High |
| Glycosylation | None | High mannose; not human | Human-compatible |
| Disulphide bonds | Often mismatched | Usually correct | Correct |
| Secretion | Poor (mostly intracellular) | Good | Good |
| Endotoxin | Yes (LPS) | No | No |
| Examples | Insulin, GH, IFN-β1b | Hepatitis B vaccine, insulin | EPO, Factor VIII, mAbs, tPA |

### Batch vs fed-batch vs continuous fermentation

| Feature | Batch | Fed-batch | Continuous |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nutrients | Added at start only | Added during run | Added and removed continuously |
| Volume | Constant | Increases | Constant |
| Duration | Fixed (hours–days) | Extended | Indefinite (weeks–months) |
| Contamination risk | Lower | Lower | Higher |
| Main use | Beer, wine, vaccines | Penicillin, recombinant proteins | Wastewater, some amino acids |

### Biosimilar vs originator biologic

| Feature | Originator biologic | Biosimilar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First approval | Full clinical trial package | Comparability data + abbreviated clinical |
| Approval pathway | BLA (FDA), MAA (EMA), NDA (CDSCO) | Abbreviated BLA (FDA 351(k)), CHMP guideline |
| Manufacturing | Original cell line and process | Different cell line; must demonstrate comparability |
| Identical to reference? | Is the reference | Highly similar, not identical |
| Naming | INN alone | INN + suffix (US); same INN (EU) |
| Cost | High | Lower (20–80% reduction) |

### Chromatography types used in biopharmaceutical purification

| Type | Basis of separation | Ligand/stationary phase | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Affinity | Specific interaction (Protein A–Fc) | Protein A, substrate analogues, His-tag Ni resin | Highest specificity; first capture step |
| Ion exchange | Charge | DEAE (anion), CM/SP (cation) | Most impurity removal |
| Size exclusion | Molecular size | Sephadex, Superose | Aggregate removal, polishing, analytical |
| Hydrophobic interaction | Hydrophobicity | Butyl-, phenyl-Sepharose | Used at high salt (after ammonium sulphate) |

## Text diagrams

### Hybridoma technology flowchart

```text
Immunise mouse with antigen
          ↓
Collect spleen cells (3–5 days after last boost)
          ↓
Fuse with HGPRT-negative myeloma cells using PEG
          ↓
Culture in HAT medium
  ├── Unfused myeloma cells DIE (blocked main pathway, no salvage)
  ├── Unfused B cells DIE (limited lifespan)
  └── Hybridomas SURVIVE (use salvage pathway from B-cell nucleus)
          ↓
Dilute into 96-well plates (1 cell/well) → clonal expansion
          ↓
Screen supernatants by ELISA for specific antibody
          ↓
Re-clone positive wells → confirm monoclonality
          ↓
Scale up → bioreactor or mouse ascites → Protein A purification
          ↓
MONOCLONAL ANTIBODY
```

### Penicillin production summary

```text
P. chrysogenum spore stock
          ↓
Shake flask → seed fermenter
          ↓
Production fermenter (fed-batch, 25–26°C, pH 6.0–6.5)
Medium: corn steep liquor + lactose + phenylacetic acid (Pen G precursor)
          ↓
Ferment 6–8 days (penicillin accumulates in idiophase)
          ↓
Mycelium removed by filtration
Broth acidified (pH 2–3) → extract into organic solvent
Re-extract into aqueous buffer (pH 7) → charcoal treatment → crystallise
          ↓
Potassium penicillin G crystal
```

## Recombinant therapeutic proteins reference table

| Product | Gene/protein | Host system | Key indication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Insulin (Humulin, Novolog) | Proinsulin | *E. coli* or yeast | Type 1 and type 2 diabetes |
| Somatropin (Genotropin) | hGH (191 aa) | *E. coli* | GH deficiency, Turner syndrome |

## Scoring tips

1. **Draw the bioreactor.** Two boxes with components labelled (sparger, impeller, baffles, probes, jacket) is worth 3–4 marks in a 10-mark fermentation question.
2. **Write the PCR cycle as three named steps with their temperatures.** Denaturation 95°C, annealing 55–65°C, extension 72°C. Add: Taq polymerase from *Thermus aquaticus*; Mullis 1983 Nobel Prize 1993.
3. **For hybridoma, explain HAT selection clearly.** State what aminopterin does (blocks de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis) and why the myeloma cells die (they cannot use the salvage pathway due to their HGPRT mutation).
4. **For biosimilar questions, use the word "comparability."** Regulators ask for a comparability exercise; the drug is highly similar, not identical, because living cells cannot produce identical molecules.
5. **State units and limits for quality control.** Endotoxin limit: 5 EU/kg per dose (IV products). Residual host cell DNA: < 10 ng per dose (WHO). These numbers earn marks in a 10-mark QC or DSP question.
6. **Know the virus clearance steps.** Low pH (inactivates enveloped viruses), solvent/detergent (enveloped), viral nanofiltration 20 nm (enveloped and some non-enveloped). Two orthogonal steps required; ICH Q5A is the guiding document.

questions.answer:
1. Gene cloning is the technique of isolating a specific gene and making many identical copies of it inside a host cell.
2. Step 1 — Isolation: The DNA source is lysed and total genomic DNA is extracted. If the protein sequence is known, the gene can be synthesised chemically (oligonucleotide synthesis).
3. Step 2 — Restriction digestion: Both the target DNA and the vector (usually a plasmid) are treated with the SAME Type II restriction enzyme, which recognises a specific palindromic sequence and cuts both strands, producing complementary single-stranded sticky ends (cohesive ends).
4. Step 3 — Ligation: The insert DNA and linearised vector are mixed with T4 DNA ligase and ATP. The sticky ends of insert and vector anneal by base pairing, and T4 DNA ligase catalyses phosphodiester bond formation, creating a covalent recombinant plasmid.
5. Step 4 — Transformation: The recombinant plasmid is introduced into competent host bacteria (usually E. coli) made permeable by CaCl2 treatment (chemical competence) or electroporation. The cells are heat-shocked briefly to facilitate uptake.
6. Step 5 — Selection: Transformed cells are plated on agar containing an antibiotic corresponding to the vector's resistance gene. Only cells that have taken up the vector grow. To identify clones containing the insert (versus re-ligated vector), blue-white screening is used: the multiple cloning site disrupts the lacZ gene, so insert-containing colonies are white and vector-only colonies are blue on X-gal/IPTG plates. Positive clones are confirmed by colony PCR or restriction mapping.
7. Types of vectors: plasmids (up to 10 kb insert), bacteriophage lambda (10–20 kb), cosmids (35–45 kb), BACs (100–300 kb), and YACs (up to 1000 kb). A vector must carry an origin of replication, selectable markers, and a multiple cloning site.
8. Expression vectors additionally carry a promoter, ribosome binding site, and terminator to drive protein production from the cloned gene.
9. The method has applications in producing recombinant proteins (insulin, vaccines), gene therapy vectors, and genomic libraries.

questions.answer:
1. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is an in-vitro technique for amplifying a specific DNA sequence exponentially, developed by Kary Mullis in 1983 (Nobel Prize 1993).
2. Principle: by repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension, a target DNA sequence is copied exponentially so that 2n copies are made after n cycles. After 30 cycles, one copy becomes approximately 10^9 copies.
3. Components: (a) Template DNA — the source containing the sequence to amplify; (b) Two oligonucleotide primers — short single-stranded DNA molecules (20–30 bases each) complementary to the flanking sequences on opposite strands; (c) Thermostable DNA polymerase — Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, which survives the 95°C denaturation step; (d) dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP) — building blocks; (e) Buffer containing Mg2+, which is a cofactor for Taq polymerase.
4. Three-step cycle: (i) Denaturation at 95°C — the two strands of dsDNA separate; (ii) Annealing at 55–65°C — primers bind to their complementary sequences on each single strand; (iii) Extension at 72°C — Taq polymerase extends from the 3' end of each primer, synthesising a new complementary strand.
5. Products double with each cycle; early cycles produce variable-length products; from cycle 3 onwards the dominant product is exactly the length between the two primers.
6. Applications — Diagnosis: RT-PCR detects viral RNA (HIV, SARS-CoV-2, influenza) after reverse transcription; PCR diagnoses tuberculosis, hepatitis B/C, and many bacterial infections from clinical samples; PCR-based tests replaced culture for many infectious diseases because of speed and sensitivity.
7. Applications — Forensics: DNA fingerprinting (STR analysis) from tiny crime-scene samples such as a single hair root or bloodstain; parentage and identity testing; disaster victim identification.
8. Applications — Cloning: PCR amplifies a gene of interest before inserting it into a vector; restriction sites or recombination sequences can be built into the primers to facilitate directional cloning.
9. Applications — Quantitative PCR (qPCR): monitors fluorescence after each cycle; allows quantitation of starting template amount; used for gene expression studies and viral load measurement.
10. Applications — Prenatal diagnosis: fetal DNA from chorionic villi or amniotic fluid is amplified to detect mutations (e.g. sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis).

questions.answer:
1. Restriction endonucleases are bacterial enzymes that protect bacteria from foreign DNA by cutting it at specific sequences. They are classified into three types.
2. Type I: recognise specific sequences, methylate at that site, and cut randomly at a distant location (up to 1000 bp away); require ATP and S-adenosylmethionine; not useful for rDNA work because the cut site is unpredictable.
3. Type II: recognise a specific 4–8 bp palindromic sequence and cut at or near that site; require only Mg2+; produce defined fragments every time; this predictability makes them the workhorse of all rDNA technology.
4. Type III: recognise asymmetric sequences and cut a fixed distance (24–26 bp) downstream; require ATP; produce fragments with 2-nt 5' overhangs; not routinely used in cloning.
5. Role of Type II enzymes: when both the target DNA and the vector are cut with the same enzyme, they produce identical complementary sticky ends. These ends anneal by base pairing and are then permanently joined by DNA ligase. EcoRI cuts 5'-GAATTC-3' between G and A to give 4-nt 5' overhangs; HindIII cuts AAGCTT; BamHI cuts GGATCC. When a blunt-end cutter such as SmaI is used, blunt-end ligation is performed.
6. Naming: EcoRI = Escherichia coli, restriction enzyme I (first type II enzyme from that strain).
7. Sanger dideoxy sequencing principle: dideoxynucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) lack the 3'-hydroxyl group. When a ddNTP is incorporated by DNA polymerase, chain extension stops because no next phosphodiester bond can form.
8. Procedure: a primer anneals to a known sequence on the denatured template; DNA polymerase extends the primer in the presence of all four dNTPs plus a small proportion of one ddNTP (e.g. ddATP). At each position where A should be incorporated, the growing chain may either continue (if dATP is incorporated) or terminate (if ddATP is incorporated), producing a family of fragments all ending at an A position. Four separate reactions (one for each ddNTP) generate four ladders.
9. Gel electrophoresis (polyacrylamide) separates the fragments by size; reading the bands from bottom (smallest, nearest 5' end) to top gives the sequence.
10. Modern automated Sanger sequencing uses four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (each colour for one base) in a single reaction, with capillary electrophoresis and laser detection; it can sequence 800–1000 bases per run.
11. Next-generation sequencing (NGS): massively parallel sequencing of millions of fragments simultaneously on platforms such as Illumina; allows whole-genome sequencing in days.

questions.answer:
A vector is a DNA molecule used to carry a foreign gene into a host cell and allow it to replicate.
Essential features: (1) An origin of replication (ori) so the vector replicates autonomously inside the host. (2) One or more selectable markers — usually antibiotic resistance genes (e.g. ampicillin, kanamycin) — so cells containing the vector can be selected. (3) A multiple cloning site (polylinker) containing many restriction enzyme recognition sequences in a cluster where the insert is introduced. (4) Small size for efficient transformation.
Types of vectors: (a) Plasmids — circular dsDNA, 2–10 kb insert capacity; most common for small genes; examples: pUC19, pBR322. (b) Bacteriophage lambda — infects E. coli; nonessential central region of the phage genome replaced by insert; capacity 10–20 kb; high transformation efficiency. (c) Cosmids — plasmids containing the lambda cos site; packaged into phage heads for delivery into E. coli; capacity 35–45 kb; used for genomic libraries. (d) Bacterial artificial chromosomes (BAC) — based on the F plasmid of E. coli; capacity 100–300 kb; used in the Human Genome Project. (e) Yeast artificial chromosomes (YAC) — carry yeast centromere, telomeres and autonomously replicating sequence (ARS); capacity up to 1000 kb; used for very large genomic inserts. Expression vectors additionally contain a strong inducible promoter, ribosome binding site and terminator, allowing the cloned gene to be expressed as protein in the host.

questions.answer:
Gel electrophoresis separates molecules by size. DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive electrode through an agarose or polyacrylamide gel under an electric field; smaller molecules travel faster. Agarose gel is used for DNA (100 bp to 20 kb); polyacrylamide gel gives higher resolution for small DNA (sequencing) and proteins. DNA is visualised by ethidium bromide staining and UV fluorescence; proteins by Coomassie or silver stain.
Southern blotting (described by Edwin Southern, 1975): separates DNA by gel electrophoresis → denatures in alkali → transfers to a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane by capillary flow → membrane is hybridised with a labelled (radioactive or chemiluminescent) DNA or RNA probe complementary to the gene of interest → bands detected by autoradiography. Used to detect specific DNA sequences, restriction fragment length polymorphisms, and gene mutations.
Northern blotting: separates RNA by denaturing gel electrophoresis → transfers to membrane → hybridised with a labelled DNA probe → detects specific mRNA species and measures gene expression.
Western blotting: separates proteins by SDS-PAGE → transfers to nitrocellulose → probed with a specific primary antibody → detected with enzyme-conjugated secondary antibody and substrate. Used for protein identification and to confirm HIV serology. Mnemonic: SNoW DRoP — S = DNA, N = RNA, W = protein.

questions.answer:
Restriction endonucleases are bacterial DNA-cutting enzymes that recognise specific DNA sequences and cleave both strands. They form part of the bacterial restriction-modification system protecting against foreign DNA.
Type I: recognise and methylate at one site; cut randomly at a distant site (1000+ bp away); require ATP and S-adenosylmethionine; produce unpredictable fragments. Not used for cloning.
Type II: recognise a specific palindromic 4–8 bp sequence and cut at or near that site; require only Mg2+; produce specific fragments every time; examples include EcoRI (cuts GAATTC, 4-nt 5' sticky ends), HindIII, BamHI, SmaI (blunt end). These are the workhorse enzymes of rDNA technology.
Type III: recognise asymmetric sequences; cut 24–26 bp downstream; require ATP; produce 2-nt 5' overhangs; not routinely used in cloning.
Why Type II: they produce predictable fragments with defined sticky ends. When the same enzyme is used to cut both the insert and the vector, the sticky ends are complementary and can anneal before being joined by DNA ligase. This predictability and the availability of hundreds of characterised Type II enzymes make them indispensable for constructing recombinant DNA molecules.

questions.answer:
Sanger sequencing principle: dideoxynucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) lack the 3'-hydroxyl group that is required to form the next phosphodiester bond. When a ddNTP is incorporated into a growing DNA strand by DNA polymerase, extension terminates at that position.
Procedure: a primer hybridises to the template; DNA polymerase extends the primer in the presence of all four dNTPs plus a low concentration of one ddNTP. At every position where that base should be incorporated, extension may stop (ddNTP incorporated) or continue (dNTP incorporated), producing a mixture of fragments of all possible lengths each ending at that base. Four reactions (one per ddNTP) are run separately and electrophoresed on polyacrylamide gel; reading the ladder from shortest (bottom) to longest (top) gives the sequence.
Modern automated Sanger: four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (different colour per base) in one tube; capillary electrophoresis; laser detector reads fluorescence order as fragments pass. Reads 800–1000 bases per run; turnaround 1–2 days.
Next-generation sequencing (NGS): millions of DNA fragments are sequenced simultaneously (massively parallel). Library preparation fragments the genome; adapters are ligated; clusters are amplified on a flowcell; sequencing-by-synthesis with fluorescent nucleotides reads each cluster. A whole human genome is sequenced in 1–3 days at a cost of a few hundred dollars. NGS is used for whole-genome sequencing, RNA-seq, metagenomics, cancer mutation profiling, and pharmacogenomics.

questions.answer:
PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro. Components: template DNA, two oligonucleotide primers (20–30 bases) flanking the target, thermostable Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus), all four dNTPs, Mg2+-containing buffer.
Cycle (25–35 cycles): (1) Denaturation at 95°C — double-stranded DNA melts into single strands. (2) Annealing at 55–65°C — primers bind to their complementary sequences. (3) Extension at 72°C — Taq polymerase synthesises new DNA from each primer's 3' end.
After 30 cycles, one target copy becomes approximately 10^9 copies. The dominant product is exactly the length between the two primer binding sites.
Applications in molecular diagnostics: (a) Infectious disease detection — PCR detects bacterial and viral DNA/RNA directly from clinical samples; RT-PCR converts viral RNA to cDNA first; used for HIV viral load, hepatitis B/C, tuberculosis, SARS-CoV-2, influenza. (b) Prenatal genetic diagnosis — fetal cells from amniotic fluid or CVS amplified to detect inherited mutations (sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, thalassaemia). (c) Oncology — detection of BCR-ABL translocation in CML, BRAF mutations in melanoma, minimal residual disease monitoring. (d) Forensics — STR profiling for identity and parentage. (e) Food safety and species authentication.

questions.answer:
1. The choice of expression system is determined by the complexity, size, and post-translational modification requirements of the target protein.
2. Prokaryotic systems — E. coli: grows rapidly (20 min doubling time), inexpensive culture media, high protein yield (up to 30% of total cell protein), well-characterised genetics. Key components of an E. coli expression vector: a strong inducible promoter (T7, tac), ribosome binding site (Shine-Dalgarno sequence), antibiotic resistance marker, and multiple cloning site. IPTG (isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside) induces the lac promoter. Main limitations: cannot glycosylate proteins; foreign proteins often form insoluble inclusion bodies (require refolding); endotoxin contamination must be removed; some eukaryotic disulphide bond patterns are incorrectly formed.
3. Eukaryotic systems: (a) Yeast (Saccharomyces, Pichia pastoris) — glycosylates proteins (high-mannose glycans), secretes products into medium, grows well, no endotoxin, GRAS status. Glycans differ from human. Used for HBsAg vaccine, insulin. (b) Insect cells/baculovirus — good post-translational modifications; virus-like particle assembly; difficult to scale. (c) CHO cells — most widely used for therapeutic glycoproteins; produce human-compatible complex glycans; correct disulphide bonds and secretion; slow growth, high cost, viral clearance required. Used for EPO, Factor VIII, mAbs, tPA.
4. Recombinant human insulin: insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains (A: 21, B: 30) linked by two interchain and one intrachain disulphide bonds.
5. Production in E. coli — proinsulin route (preferred industrial method): a synthetic proinsulin gene (without introns) is designed, codon-optimised for E. coli, and cloned into an expression vector. It is expressed as a fusion protein (e.g. with a signal peptide or affinity tag), purified, and the fusion partner cleaved. The proinsulin is then treated in vitro with trypsin and carboxypeptidase B to remove the C-peptide and produce mature insulin. Disulphide bonds are formed by controlled oxidative refolding.
6. Production in yeast: proinsulin is expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae or Pichia pastoris under the control of a strong promoter; the protein is secreted into the medium (simplifying purification), and the C-peptide is removed enzymatically. Yeast production eliminates endotoxin concerns.
7. Advantages over animal insulin: identical sequence to human insulin, no immunogenic differences, unlimited supply without dependence on slaughterhouse material.
8. Insulin analogues (lispro, aspart, glargine) are made by site-directed mutagenesis of the proinsulin gene before expression to alter the pharmacokinetic profile.

questions.answer:
1. Recombinant erythropoietin (EPO): Erythropoietin is a 165-amino acid glycoprotein hormone produced by peritubular fibroblasts of the kidney; it stimulates proliferation and differentiation of erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow.
2. Why mammalian cells: EPO carries three N-linked and one O-linked glycan chains that account for 40% of its molecular mass. Glycosylation is essential for its in vivo half-life and biological activity — it determines clearance by asialoglycoprotein receptors in the liver. E. coli cannot glycosylate; yeast glycans are immunogenic (high mannose); CHO cells produce complex glycans close to human patterns.
3. Production: the EPO gene is expressed in CHO cells. The protein is secreted into the conditioned medium and purified by ion exchange and reverse-phase chromatography.
4. Uses of EPO (epoetin alfa): anaemia of chronic kidney disease (most common use), chemotherapy-induced anaemia, anaemia in HIV patients on zidovudine, pre-surgical autologous blood donation.
5. Darbepoetin alfa is an engineered EPO analogue with two additional N-glycosylation sites, giving a threefold longer half-life; allows weekly or bi-weekly dosing instead of three times per week.
6. Misuse: EPO is abused by endurance athletes to increase haematocrit and oxygen-carrying capacity. This causes polycythaemia, hyperviscosity, hypertension, and risk of thromboembolism including stroke and myocardial infarction. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) prohibits its use.
7. Interferons: interferon-alpha (IFN-α) is produced by leucocytes; antiviral and antiproliferative. Recombinant IFN-α2a and IFN-α2b are expressed in E. coli. PEGylation (Peg-IFN-α2a and Peg-IFN-α2b) adds polyethylene glycol chains to extend half-life from 8 hours to 3–4 days, allowing once-weekly dosing.
8. Uses of IFN-α: chronic hepatitis B and C (now largely replaced by direct-acting antivirals), hairy cell leukaemia, Kaposi sarcoma, melanoma.
9. Interferon-beta (IFN-β): IFN-β1a (CHO cells, same sequence as natural IFN-β) and IFN-β1b (E. coli, Cys17→Ser mutation for stability, slightly different from natural) are both used in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; they modulate the immune response.
10. Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ1b, Actimmune; E. coli): activates macrophage killing; used in chronic granulomatous disease and severe malignant osteopetrosis.
11. Adverse effects common to all interferons: flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, myalgia, headache) — the most common, occurring in almost all patients; depression and mood disorders; myelosuppression (low WBC, platelets); raised liver enzymes; injection-site reactions. Specific to IFN-β: injection-site necrosis; neutralising antibodies in some patients.

questions.answer:
1. Haemophilia A is caused by deficiency of coagulation Factor VIII; haemophilia B by deficiency of Factor IX. Both are X-linked recessive bleeding disorders.
2. Plasma-derived Factor VIII: before recombinant technology, Factor VIII was extracted from pooled plasma of thousands of donors. Contamination with HIV and hepatitis C transmitted these viruses widely during the 1980s, before testing became available.
3. Recombinant Factor VIII (rFVIII, e.g. Advate, Recombinate): expressed in CHO or BHK cells because Factor VIII (2332 amino acids) is a large glycoprotein requiring correct glycosylation, disulphide bonds, and von Willebrand factor binding. It is purified by immunoaffinity chromatography. Viral clearance steps are still included as a precaution.
4. Advantages: eliminates risk of blood-borne viral transmission; consistent potency; unlimited supply; no pooled plasma needed.
5. Extended half-life Factor VIII products: PEGylation or fusion with the Fc domain of IgG (efmoroctocog alfa) or with albumin extends the half-life from 8–12 hours to 19–36 hours, reducing the injection frequency from every 2–3 days to weekly or less.
6. Recombinant Factor IX (rFIX, Benefix): expressed in CHO cells; used in haemophilia B. Gene therapy with adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivering the Factor IX gene is now approved (Hemgenix) and can cure haemophilia B with a single infusion.
7. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA): a serine protease produced naturally by endothelial cells; cleaves plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves fibrin clots. The natural protein (527 amino acids) is heavily glycosylated and expressed in CHO cells.
8. Mechanism: tPA binds to fibrin at the clot site (fibrin specificity reduces systemic plasminogen activation and bleeding). tPA converts fibrin-bound plasminogen to plasmin; plasmin degrades fibrin and dissolves the clot.
9. Uses: acute myocardial infarction (within 12 hours of onset, ideally within 1 hour); acute ischaemic stroke (within 4.5 hours of onset, contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke); massive pulmonary embolism.
10. Variants: reteplase (expressed in E. coli; non-glycosylated, so shorter half-life offset by double bolus; easier to administer); tenecteplase (single bolus; higher fibrin specificity; longer half-life).
11. The key advance of recombinant tPA over streptokinase (a bacterial enzyme): fibrin specificity reduces systemic fibrinogen depletion and bleeding risk; recombinant product eliminates the antigenic concern of a bacterial protein.
questions.question: Describe recombinant coagulation factors for haemophilia and tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). Include the host system, mechanism of action, clinical uses, and advantages over plasma-derived products.

questions.answer:
E. coli advantages: extremely fast growth (doubling time 20 minutes), well-understood genetics, cheap defined media, very high yields (up to 30% total cell protein), no cold chain needed during fermentation, no endotoxin in the product if done correctly. Suitable for: (a) recombinant human insulin (no glycosylation required; proinsulin route); (b) recombinant growth hormone (somatropin; no glycosylation required); (c) G-CSF (filgrastim; not glycosylated in the therapeutic form); (d) IFN-β1b and IFN-α2b.
Unsuitability for glycoproteins: E. coli lacks the cellular machinery (endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus) needed for N-linked and O-linked glycosylation. Glycosylation is not simply decoration — it determines protein folding, stability, clearance rate, and in vivo half-life. Unglycosylated EPO, for example, has a very short half-life and poor bioactivity.
Examples of glycoproteins needing mammalian cells: (a) Erythropoietin (EPO) — 40% of its mass is carbohydrate; glycosylation is essential for in vivo activity and prevents renal filtration; produced in CHO cells. (b) Coagulation Factor VIII — large glycoprotein, correct glycosylation needed for stability and von Willebrand factor interaction; produced in CHO or BHK cells. (c) Monoclonal antibodies — Fc-region glycosylation needed for ADCC and CDC effector functions; produced in CHO cells.
questions.question: Why is E. coli preferred for many recombinant proteins but unsuitable for glycoproteins? Give two examples of each category.

questions.answer:
Inclusion bodies are dense, insoluble aggregates of recombinant protein that form in E. coli when the protein is expressed at very high levels and cannot fold correctly or is expressed faster than the folding machinery can process it. They appear as bright refractile granules under phase-contrast microscopy. Inclusion bodies protect the protein from protease degradation and can be isolated easily by low-speed centrifugation, so they represent a relatively pure starting material.
Recovery and refolding procedure: (1) Cell disruption — cells are lysed by high-pressure homogenisation or French press. (2) Centrifugation — the dense inclusion bodies pellet at 5,000–10,000 g, while soluble proteins remain in the supernatant. The pellet is washed to remove contaminating membrane fragments and soluble proteins. (3) Solubilisation — the inclusion body pellet is dissolved in a high concentration of a denaturant: 6–8 M urea or 6 M guanidinium hydrochloride (Gdm-HCl), which disrupts non-covalent interactions and linearises the protein. Reducing agent (DTT or beta-mercaptoethanol) is added to break incorrect disulphide bonds. (4) Refolding — the denaturant is slowly removed by dilution or dialysis. As denaturant concentration falls, the protein collapses and refolds. For proteins with disulphide bonds, an oxidative refolding system (a mixture of oxidised and reduced glutathione) allows correct disulphide bond formation. (5) Purification — the refolded protein is purified by chromatography.
This process works well for insulin (proinsulin from inclusion bodies) and human growth hormone.
questions.question: What are inclusion bodies? Describe how recombinant proteins trapped in inclusion bodies are recovered and refolded.

questions.answer:
Colony-stimulating factors are cytokines that stimulate the proliferation, differentiation, and survival of haematopoietic progenitor cells. Two are clinically important recombinant products.
1. G-CSF (Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor, filgrastim): a 174-amino acid protein produced by filgrastim (Met-G-CSF) expressed in E. coli. Its natural counterpart is glycosylated, but unglycosylated filgrastim is biologically active with a slightly shorter half-life. Mechanism: G-CSF binds the G-CSF receptor on neutrophil precursors, activates JAK2/STAT3 signalling, and drives proliferation and differentiation of granulocyte progenitors in bone marrow; also mobilises mature neutrophils from bone marrow into the bloodstream. Uses: (a) Prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia — given after each chemotherapy cycle to shorten the duration of neutropenia and reduce the risk of febrile neutropenia; (b) Mobilisation of haematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow into peripheral blood before collection for stem cell transplantation; (c) Severe chronic neutropenia.
2. Pegfilgrastim: PEGylated G-CSF with a much longer half-life (allowing a single injection per chemotherapy cycle rather than daily injections for 10–14 days).
3. GM-CSF (Granulocyte-Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor, sargramostim): expressed in yeast; stimulates neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages. Used after bone marrow transplantation and in chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression. More inflammatory adverse effects than G-CSF. Adverse effects of both: bone pain (from marrow expansion), fever, splenomegaly with long use.
questions.question: Write a note on colony-stimulating factors (CSFs): types, production, mechanism of action and clinical uses.

questions.answer:
Transgenic animal expression (pharming): the gene of interest is placed under the control of a mammary gland-specific promoter (e.g. beta-casein or whey acidic protein promoter) and inserted into the germline of a farm animal (goat, sheep, cow, rabbit) by pronuclear microinjection or somatic cell nuclear transfer. Founder animals transmit the transgene to their offspring. The recombinant protein is secreted into milk at high concentrations (1–10 g/L) and can be harvested continuously by milking. Example: antithrombin III (ATryn) from transgenic goats (approved by EMA and FDA). Advantages: potentially unlimited scale using existing dairy infrastructure, correct post-translational modifications, low manufacturing cost per gram. Disadvantages: long development time (years to establish and breed a herd), animal welfare concerns, risk of transgene spread to the environment, complex purification from milk, regulatory uncertainty.
Plant-based expression (molecular pharming): the gene is introduced into plant cells via Agrobacterium tumefaciens (Ti plasmid vector) or biolistics (gene gun). Stable transformants are regenerated into whole plants; the protein accumulates in leaves, seeds or tubers. Transient expression (using tobacco mosaic virus vectors in tobacco leaves) allows faster production. Advantages: scalable by growing more plants, no mammalian pathogens, low raw material cost. Disadvantages: plant glycans (alpha-1,3-fucose, beta-1,2-xylose) differ from human glycans and may be immunogenic; regulatory pathway is not fully defined; protein extraction from plant tissue is challenging.
questions.question: Describe transgenic animals and plant-based expression systems for recombinant protein production.

questions.answer:
PEGylation is the covalent attachment of one or more polyethylene glycol (PEG) polymer chains to a therapeutic protein or other molecule. PEG is a flexible, water-soluble, non-toxic, non-immunogenic polymer of ethylene oxide units [-(CH2-CH2-O)n-].
Mechanism by which PEGylation prolongs half-life: (1) Increased hydrodynamic radius — the PEG chains create a large water shell around the protein, increasing its effective size in solution; this reduces renal filtration (glomerular filtration retains molecules >60 kDa). (2) Reduced immunogenicity — PEG shields antigenic epitopes and reduces recognition by antibodies and proteases. (3) Reduced receptor-mediated clearance — shielding of the protein surface reduces receptor-mediated uptake. PEGylation typically extends the half-life by 3- to 20-fold.
Chemistry: PEG-NHS ester or PEG-maleimide reacts with lysine ε-amino groups or cysteine thiol groups on the protein. Site-specific PEGylation using engineered non-natural amino acids is a newer approach.
Examples: (a) Peg-IFN-α2a (Pegasys) and Peg-IFN-α2b (Peg-Intron) — once-weekly dosing instead of thrice-weekly for hepatitis C; (b) Pegfilgrastim (Neulasta) — once per chemotherapy cycle instead of daily G-CSF injections; (c) Certolizumab pegol (Cimzia) — PEGylated Fab fragment of anti-TNF antibody for rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's; (d) Darbepoetin alfa is not PEGylated but achieves extended half-life by hyperglycosylation — an example of an alternative strategy.
questions.question: Write a note on PEGylation of biopharmaceuticals with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Hybridoma technology, developed by Köhler and Milstein in 1975 (Nobel Prize 1984), allows production of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) — antibodies from a single B-cell clone, all identical in sequence and specificity.
2. Steps in hybridoma production: (a) Immunisation — a mouse is injected with the antigen (purified protein, cell, or hapten-carrier conjugate) with Freund's adjuvant; a booster is given 2–3 weeks later; the mouse is sacrificed 3–5 days after the final boost. (b) Spleen cell isolation — the spleen is rich in activated B cells secreting antibodies against the immunogen. (c) Cell fusion — spleen cells are mixed with HGPRT-negative, non-antibody-secreting mouse myeloma cells (SP2/0 or NS0) in the presence of polyethylene glycol (PEG), which destabilises membranes and allows cell fusion. Hybridomas form at low frequency (~1 per 10^5 cells). (d) HAT selection — cells are cultured in HAT medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine. Aminopterin blocks the de novo pathway of nucleotide synthesis (blocking DHFR). Unfused myeloma cells cannot use the salvage pathway (they lack HGPRT) and die. Unfused B cells die naturally within 1–2 weeks. Hybridomas survive because they receive the working HGPRT gene from the B-cell nucleus and can use the salvage pathway. (e) Cloning — hybridoma cells are diluted into 96-well plates at approximately one cell per well; each growing colony is a clone derived from a single cell. (f) Screening — culture supernatants are tested by ELISA to identify those containing antibody that binds the antigen. (g) Production — positive clones are expanded in bioreactors or as mouse ascites tumours; antibody is purified by Protein A/G affinity chromatography.
3. Limitation of murine mAbs: patients make a human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA) response, which neutralises the drug and can cause hypersensitivity reactions after repeated dosing.
4. Chimeric antibodies (-ximab): the mouse variable regions (VH and VL, which carry the antigen-binding specificity) are joined to human constant regions (Fc). About 65% human. Example: rituximab, cetuximab, infliximab. Reduced HAMA response but anti-chimeric antibodies still possible.
5. Humanised antibodies (-zumab): only the CDR loops (the three short antigen-contact loops in each variable domain) from the mouse antibody are grafted onto a human antibody framework by CDR grafting. The framework residues are human. About 95% human. Examples: trastuzumab (anti-HER2), bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), alemtuzumab, omalizumab. Minimal immunogenicity.
6. Fully human antibodies (-umab): produced by phage display (a large library of human VH and VL genes displayed on bacteriophage surface; antigen-binding clones selected by panning) or transgenic mice carrying human immunoglobulin gene loci (Medarex/UltiMAb). 100% human. Examples: adalimumab, denosumab, ustekinumab. No HAMA response.
questions.question: Describe hybridoma technology in detail. How are chimeric, humanised and fully human monoclonal antibodies produced?

questions.answer:
1. Monoclonal antibodies are the largest and fastest-growing class of biopharmaceuticals. Naming: source suffix (-o- murine, -xi- chimeric, -zu- humanised, -u- human) + target infix + -mab suffix.
2. Anti-cancer mAbs: (a) Rituximab (chimeric anti-CD20): binds CD20, a cell-surface antigen on B lymphocytes. CD20 is expressed on most B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHL) and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Rituximab triggers ADCC, CDC and direct apoptosis. First mAb approved for cancer (1997). Also used in rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune conditions. ADR: progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy (PML), infusion reactions, reactivation of hepatitis B. (b) Trastuzumab (humanised anti-HER2/neu, Herceptin): HER2 is overexpressed in 20–25% of breast cancers; also some gastric cancers. Trastuzumab blocks HER2 signalling, inhibits proliferation, and recruits immune effectors. ADR: cardiotoxicity (reduced left ventricular ejection fraction) — LVEF must be monitored; contraindicated with anthracyclines. (c) Bevacizumab (humanised anti-VEGF, Avastin): binds and neutralises all VEGF-A isoforms, preventing angiogenesis. Used in colorectal, non-small-cell lung, ovarian, and other cancers. ADR: hypertension, impaired wound healing, thromboembolism, bowel perforation, proteinuria. (d) Cetuximab (chimeric anti-EGFR, Erbitux): blocks EGFR; used in KRAS wild-type colorectal cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. ADR: acneiform skin rash (a marker of response — patients with rash respond better). (e) Pembrolizumab (humanised anti-PD-1, Keytruda): checkpoint inhibitor; blocks PD-1, restoring T-cell killing of tumour cells. Used in multiple solid tumours. ADR: immune-related adverse effects (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, skin reactions).
3. mAbs in autoimmune disease: (a) Adalimumab (fully human anti-TNF-α, Humira): binds and neutralises TNF-alpha; used in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, psoriasis. Best-selling drug in the world for many years. ADR: reactivation of latent TB (screen before starting), serious infections, demyelinating disease, lymphoma risk. (b) Infliximab (chimeric anti-TNF-α, Remicade): same mechanism and uses as adalimumab; given by infusion. ADR: same as adalimumab plus infusion reactions. (c) Omalizumab (humanised anti-IgE, Xolair): binds free IgE, preventing mast cell degranulation; used in severe allergic asthma and chronic urticaria. (d) Ustekinumab (fully human anti-IL-12/23, Stelara): used in psoriasis, Crohn's.
4. ADC (antibody-drug conjugate) example: ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) — trastuzumab linked to emtansine (a microtubule inhibitor) through a stable linker; used in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer; targets the cytotoxic payload directly to HER2-expressing cells.
questions.question: Classify and describe therapeutic monoclonal antibodies used in oncology and autoimmune diseases. Include targets, indications, and adverse effects.

questions.answer:
1. Recombinant vaccines use a gene encoding an antigen from the pathogen, expressed in a host system, to produce antigen that is then formulated as a vaccine. No live pathogen is involved, so safety is high.
2. Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine: the first approved recombinant subunit vaccine (1986). The gene for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is cloned and expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae under the control of a constitutive promoter. The expressed HBsAg protein self-assembles into 22-nm spherical virus-like particles (VLPs) that are non-infectious but highly immunogenic. The vaccine is purified, adsorbed to aluminium hydroxide adjuvant and formulated as an injection. Advantages: eliminated the need for plasma-derived antigen and all associated risk of blood-borne pathogen contamination; produced in large quantities; consistent quality. Used in the universal infant immunisation schedule worldwide.
3. Virus-like particles (VLPs): assemblies of viral structural proteins that mimic the natural virus in shape and size but contain no genetic material, so they cannot replicate or cause disease. VLPs are more immunogenic than soluble antigen because they mimic the repetitive surface structures of the native virus and efficiently activate B cells.
4. HPV vaccine (Gardasil, Cervarix): L1 major capsid protein of HPV types 16 and 18 (and types 6 and 11 in Gardasil) is expressed in yeast (Gardasil) or in baculovirus/insect cells (Cervarix) and self-assembles into VLPs. Protects against cervical cancer precursors caused by HPV 16 and 18 (which cause ~70% of cervical cancers); Gardasil 9 covers nine HPV types.
5. Malaria vaccine (RTS,S/Mosquirix): contains a portion of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) of Plasmodium falciparum fused to HBsAg; expressed in yeast; forms hybrid VLPs. Provides partial (30–40%) protection against clinical malaria; WHO recommends for children in sub-Saharan Africa.
6. DNA vaccines: a plasmid vector containing the antigen gene under a mammalian promoter (CMV promoter) is purified and injected into muscle or skin. Host cells express the antigen, which is presented by MHC I and II, triggering both humoral (antibody) and cellular (cytotoxic T cell) immune responses. Advantages: heat-stable (no cold chain), easy to produce and modify rapidly. Limitations: low immunogenicity in humans; concerns about plasmid integration into the host genome (addressed by design). Approved for veterinary use; several DNA vaccines for infectious diseases in clinical development.
7. Viral vector vaccines: a replication-deficient virus (commonly chimpanzee or human adenovirus, modified vaccinia Ankara — MVA) carries the antigen gene. The vector infects host cells and delivers the gene; the antigen is expressed and immune response generated. The adenovirus vector has E1 gene deleted, so it cannot replicate. Used for Ebola (VSV-based rVSV-ZEBOV), COVID-19 (ChAdOx1 nCoV-19/AstraZeneca based on chimpanzee adenovirus, Ad26.COV2.S/Johnson & Johnson based on human adenovirus 26). Pre-existing immunity to the vector can reduce efficacy — a limitation for human adenovirus vectors.
questions.question: Describe recombinant vaccines: hepatitis B, HPV, DNA vaccines and viral vector vaccines. What are virus-like particles?

questions.answer:
Sandwich ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) is used to detect and quantify antigens in a sample. It is called a sandwich because the antigen is trapped between two antibodies.
Principle: an antibody (capture antibody) coated on the microtitre plate surface captures the antigen from the sample; a second antibody (detection antibody) conjugated to an enzyme then binds a different epitope on the same antigen. Addition of enzyme substrate produces a colour change proportional to the amount of antigen.
Procedure: (1) Coat the microtitre plate wells with specific capture antibody and incubate overnight at 4°C; (2) Block non-specific binding sites with BSA, casein or skimmed milk; (3) Add sample (patient serum, urine, etc.) and incubate — antigen binds to the capture antibody; (4) Wash away unbound material; (5) Add enzyme-conjugated detection antibody (HRP or alkaline phosphatase); incubate; (6) Wash; (7) Add enzyme substrate (TMB for HRP; produces blue colour, turned yellow on stopping with acid); (8) Read absorbance at 450 nm. A standard curve from known concentrations allows quantitation.
Applications: pregnancy testing (hCG detection in urine), HIV and hepatitis serology (high-throughput blood bank screening), troponin and BNP in cardiac diagnosis, vitamin D and thyroid hormone levels, drug monitoring, detection of food allergens, cancer biomarkers (CA-125, PSA, AFP). Formats can be adapted for small molecules (haptens) using competitive ELISA.
questions.question: Describe the principle and procedure of sandwich ELISA and its diagnostic applications.

questions.answer:
IgG structure: a Y-shaped glycoprotein of approximately 150 kDa. It has two identical heavy chains (H, ~50 kDa each) and two identical light chains (L, ~25 kDa each), held together by disulphide bonds. Each chain is divided into variable (V) and constant (C) domains.
Fab region: antigen-binding fragment; consists of one VH + CH1 from the heavy chain and one VL + CL from the light chain. Each molecule has two identical Fab arms with identical antigen-binding sites.
Fc region: crystallisable fragment; consists of the two CH2 and CH3 domains of both heavy chains. Binds Fc receptors on immune effector cells (triggers ADCC), binds C1q (triggers complement), and mediates the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-dependent prolonged half-life of IgG (~21 days).
CDRs (complementarity-determining regions): within each variable domain (VH and VL), there are three CDR loops (CDR1, CDR2, CDR3). The six CDR loops from VH and VL together form the antigen-binding site and make direct contact with the antigen. CDRs are the most variable sequences in the antibody and determine antigen specificity.
Relevance in antibody engineering: CDR grafting (humanisation) transplants only the six CDR loops from a murine antibody onto a human antibody framework. This retains the binding specificity of the murine antibody while replacing ~95% of the protein with human sequence, dramatically reducing immunogenicity in patients. This is the basis of humanised mAbs (-zumab suffix), such as trastuzumab and bevacizumab.
questions.question: Describe the structure of an IgG antibody. Define CDRs and explain their relevance in antibody engineering.

questions.answer:
Radioimmunoassay (RIA): developed by Berson and Yalow, 1959 (Nobel Prize 1977). A fixed amount of radio-labelled antigen (usually 125I) competes with the unlabelled sample antigen for a limited amount of antibody. The bound/free ratio decreases as sample antigen increases — the signal is inversely proportional to antigen concentration. Very high sensitivity (pmol/L). Disadvantages: radioactive waste licence required, isotope half-life limits reagent shelf life, occupational radiation hazard. Applications: insulin assay (original use), thyroid hormones, steroid hormones, drug levels. Now largely replaced by CLIA and ELISA.
ELISA: enzyme-conjugated antibody replaces the radioactive label. Formats: sandwich (antigen detection), indirect (antibody detection in serum), competitive (small molecules). No radioactivity, stable reagents, automatable, high throughput. High sensitivity (ng/mL to pg/mL). Applications: HIV serology, hCG, troponin, BNP, drug monitoring, food allergens.
Lateral flow immunoassay (rapid diagnostic test, RDT): a nitrocellulose strip with coloured particle-labelled (gold nanoparticle or latex) antibody in the conjugate zone. Sample wicks along the strip by capillary action; antigen-labelled antibody complexes are captured at the test line (a second antibody); excess labelled antibody at the control line confirms correct flow. Results in 15–30 minutes; no equipment, electricity or laboratory needed. Lower sensitivity than ELISA. Applications: pregnancy test (hCG), COVID-19 antigen, influenza A/B, malaria, dengue, RSV, streptococcal pharyngitis.
questions.question: Compare radioimmunoassay (RIA), ELISA and lateral flow immunoassay. Give applications of each.

questions.answer:
Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs): combine the targeting specificity of a monoclonal antibody with the potent killing power of a cytotoxic small molecule (the payload). The antibody binds a tumour-specific antigen, the complex is internalised by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and the linker releases the cytotoxic drug intracellularly, killing the cell.
Components: (a) Antibody — typically an IgG1 targeting a tumour antigen; (b) Linker — cleavable (by lysosomal enzymes, pH or glutathione in the tumour cell) or non-cleavable; (c) Payload — potent cytotoxin (1–3 orders of magnitude more potent than conventional chemotherapy): maytansinoids (emtansine/DM1), auristatins (MMAE, MMAF), or camptothecin analogues (topoisomerase I inhibitors).
Examples: (a) Ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1, Kadcyla) — trastuzumab + emtansine (DM1); for HER2+ metastatic breast cancer. (b) Brentuximab vedotin (Adcetris) — anti-CD30 + MMAE; for Hodgkin lymphoma and CD30+ T-cell lymphoma. (c) Enfortumab vedotin — anti-Nectin-4 + MMAE; for urothelial cancer.
Bispecific antibodies: engineered to simultaneously bind two different antigens or epitopes. Types: (a) BiTE (bispecific T-cell engager, blinatumomab) — links CD3 on T cells to CD19 on B-cell leukaemia cells; approved for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; (b) Amivantamab (anti-EGFR × anti-MET) for non-small-cell lung cancer.
Both ADCs and bispecific antibodies represent the growing field of antibody engineering beyond the conventional IgG format.
questions.question: Write a note on ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates) and bispecific antibodies.

questions.answer:
HAT selection is the key step in hybridoma technology that selects only the desired hybridoma cells from the mixture of fused and unfused cells after PEG-mediated fusion.
HAT medium contains three components: Hypoxanthine, Aminopterin, and Thymidine.
Aminopterin is a folate antagonist that blocks dihydrofolate reductase, shutting off the de novo synthesis of purines and pyrimidines. Cells must then use the salvage pathway — hypoxanthine → IMP (requires hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, HGPRT) and thymidine → TMP (requires thymidine kinase) — to synthesise nucleotides.
What happens to each cell type: (a) Unfused myeloma cells — the myeloma line used (SP2/0, NS0) is specially engineered to be HGPRT-negative. With the de novo pathway blocked by aminopterin and without HGPRT, they cannot make purines; they die within 3–5 days. (b) Unfused spleen B cells — they have intact HGPRT, so they survive HAT medium. However, normal B cells are not immortal and naturally die in culture within 1–2 weeks. (c) Hybridomas — the hybrid between a B cell and a myeloma cell acquires the HGPRT gene from the B-cell nucleus, so it can use the salvage pathway. It also inherits the immortality of the myeloma cell. Only hybridomas survive and proliferate indefinitely in HAT medium.
After 2–3 weeks, wells containing hybridomas are screened by ELISA, and those secreting the specific antibody are identified and cloned.
questions.question: Describe HAT selection in hybridoma technology. Why do unfused myeloma cells die in HAT medium?

questions.answer:
1. A bioreactor (fermenter) is a vessel engineered to maintain optimal conditions for microbial or cell growth and product formation.
2. Stirred-tank bioreactor (STR) components: (a) Vessel — cylindrical stainless steel vessel (glass for laboratory scale); height-to-diameter ratio typically 2–3:1; working volume 70–80% of total volume; (b) Impeller/agitator — Rushton flat-blade disc turbine for bacteria and yeast (high shear, good oxygen dispersion); pitched-blade or marine impeller for fragile mammalian cells (lower shear); driven by a motor and shaft through a mechanical seal at the top or bottom; (c) Baffles — four vertical plates equally spaced on the vessel wall; break circular vortex flow and improve axial mixing; (d) Sparger — porous ring or pipe at the bottom through which sterile air or oxygen is introduced; small bubbles increase oxygen transfer rate; (e) Jacket or coils — water flows through the jacket or internal coils for heating and cooling; important because fermentation is exothermic; (f) pH electrode (glass electrode) — measures pH continuously; a feedback control system adds sterile acid (H2SO4) or base (NaOH) through peristaltic pumps; (g) Dissolved oxygen (DO) electrode (Clark polarographic) — measures dissolved oxygen; controlled by increasing stirrer speed, airflow, oxygen enrichment or pressure; (h) Temperature probe — usually a Pt100 RTD; controls jacket water temperature; (i) Foam probe and antifoam addition — foam blocks the outlet filter; a conductivity or optical probe triggers antifoam addition; (j) Exhaust gas outlet with sterile hydrophobic filter; (k) Sampling port for aseptic sample removal; (l) Inoculation port; (m) Feed lines for nutrients, acid, base, antifoam.
3. Process parameters: pH — most bacteria require 6.5–7.5; fungi 4–6; measured continuously and controlled automatically. Temperature — 25–37°C depending on organism; mammalian cells strictly 37°C. Dissolved oxygen — maintained above a critical minimum (typically 20–30% air saturation); increases in stirrer speed or airflow raise it. Nutrient feeding — fed-batch glucose feeding avoids catabolite repression and high osmolarity.
4. Scale-up: when moving from a 10-L laboratory vessel to a 10,000-L production fermenter, the same biology must work in a geometrically different environment. Key criteria: (a) Constant P/V (power input per unit volume) — maintains the same energy input for mixing per litre; (b) Constant kLa (oxygen mass transfer coefficient) — the most critical criterion because oxygen availability limits aerobic fermentations; kLa depends on stirrer speed, airflow, bubble size, and fluid properties; (c) Constant mixing time — becomes longer at large scale (up to 60–120 s in large vessels versus seconds at small scale); gradients of pH and substrate become significant; (d) Heat removal — heat production scales with volume (V) but heat transfer area scales with V^(2/3); larger vessels need more cooling coils or surface area; (e) Sterility — larger vessels are harder to sterilise; validate steam-in-place (SIP) cycles.
questions.question: Describe the design and components of a stirred-tank bioreactor. Discuss the parameters controlled during fermentation and the rationale for scale-up.

questions.answer:
1. Penicillin was the first antibiotic produced industrially; it transformed medicine. It is produced by Penicillium chrysogenum (also called P. rubens).
2. Types of penicillin: by feeding different side-chain precursors, different penicillins are produced. Phenylacetic acid or its derivatives feed into the beta-lactam ring biosynthesis and produce penicillin G (benzylpenicillin); phenoxyacetic acid produces penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin), which is acid-stable and orally active.
3. Organism: high-producing strains of P. chrysogenum have been selected by decades of mutagenesis and screening; modern strains produce up to 50,000 units/mL, compared to Fleming's original strain which produced ~4 units/mL.
4. Fermentation process: (a) Inoculum preparation — cryopreserved spores are thawed and grown in shake flasks, then transferred to a small seed fermenter, then to the production fermenter at 10% inoculum volume. (b) Medium — corn steep liquor (provides nitrogen, amino acids and growth factors), lactose or slow-release glucose (carbon source; fast-metabolised glucose suppresses penicillin synthesis via catabolite repression), phenylacetic acid or sodium phenylacetate (precursor for penicillin G side chain), mineral salts. (c) Conditions — temperature 25–26°C; pH 6.0–6.5 (critical — penicillin is unstable below pH 5 and above pH 8); DO maintained above 30% air saturation by high agitation and aeration; fed-batch mode feeding glucose and precursor continuously.
5. Fermentation kinetics: penicillin is a secondary metabolite, produced in the idiophase (stationary phase), not during active growth (trophophase). It is non-growth-associated (Luedeking-Piret model: product formation rate = β × biomass; growth coefficient α ≈ 0). Rapid growth consumes glucose at high rates and activates catabolite repression pathways that inhibit penicillin biosynthesis genes. Hence fed-batch is used to keep glucose low and growth rate slow, allowing the biosynthesis genes to operate.
6. Harvest: after 6–8 days when the penicillin titre peaks; mycelium separated by vacuum filtration or centrifugation; the clarified broth contains penicillin.
7. Extraction: (a) Broth acidified to pH 2.0–2.5 to protonate penicillin (pKa ~2.7) → it partitions into an organic solvent (amyl acetate or butyl acetate) with a distribution coefficient around 50; (b) Re-extracted into an aqueous phosphate buffer at pH 7.0 → back-extraction into organic solvent; (c) Treatment with activated charcoal to remove coloured impurities; (d) Crystallisation as potassium or sodium penicillin G salt.
8. Quality control: penicillin is assayed by HPLC and by bioassay; endotoxin tested by LAL; sterility tested by USP/BP sterility test.
questions.question: Describe penicillin production by fermentation: the organism, fermentation process, precursor feeding, extraction and the kinetics of secondary metabolite production.

questions.answer:
1. Batch fermentation: all nutrients and the inoculum are added at the beginning; nothing is added or removed (except gas) until harvest. The organism progresses through lag, exponential, deceleration and stationary phases as nutrients are consumed and inhibitory products accumulate. Simple to operate; lowest contamination risk; complete characterisation of each batch for GMP. Disadvantage: limited productivity because growth slows as nutrients deplete; non-productive time for cleaning, sterilisation and inoculation between batches. Used for beer, wine, batch vaccines.
2. Fed-batch fermentation: begins as a batch but nutrients (glucose, nitrogen source, precursor) are added continuously or intermittently during the run, while nothing is removed. The volume increases. Growth rate is controlled by the feed rate. This avoids catabolite repression at high glucose, extends the productive phase, and allows very high cell densities and product titres. Most antibiotic, amino acid and recombinant protein fermentations use fed-batch. Disadvantage: more complex control; volume increase limits final titre if the vessel fills.
3. Continuous fermentation (chemostat): fresh medium is added at a constant dilution rate D = F/V (flow rate / vessel volume); spent medium is removed at the same rate. Steady state is achieved when D = µ (specific growth rate). If D exceeds µmax, washout occurs. Advantages: steady output, easy to study kinetics. Disadvantages: highest contamination risk; strain instability with long culture times; regulatory acceptance requires extensive validation; not commonly used for pharmaceutical fermentations.
4. Upstream processing: (a) Medium formulation: defined (synthetic) media are used for GMP biopharmaceutical production to ensure lot-to-lot consistency; they contain a defined carbon source (glucose), nitrogen source (ammonium sulphate or glutamine for mammalian cells), phosphate, sulphur, trace metals and vitamins. Complex media (corn steep liquor, yeast extract, soy hydrolysate) provide growth factors cheaply and are used in antibiotic fermentations. (b) Inoculum preparation: a cryopreserved master cell bank (MCB) vial is thawed → inoculated into a T-flask or shake flask → grown → transferred to a seed fermenter (usually 1–10% the volume of the production fermenter) → grown to late exponential phase → used to inoculate the production vessel at 2–10% volume. Using a working cell bank (WCB) derived from the MCB ensures genetic consistency across batches. (c) Sterilisation: batch steam sterilisation in an autoclave at 121°C, 15 psi for 15 minutes (kill time calculated from F0 concept) for glassware and small media volumes; continuous HTST sterilisation (140°C for 20–30 seconds) for large industrial media volumes to reduce nutrient destruction; membrane filtration through 0.2 µm membranes for heat-sensitive media components, vitamins, and gases; UV radiation for surface sterilisation.

A stirred-tank bioreactor is the standard vessel for industrial fermentation.
Components and their roles: (1) Vessel — cylindrical stainless steel body with dished top and bottom; working volume 70–80% of total to allow headspace for foam; (2) Agitator/impeller — usually a Rushton turbine (flat-blade disc turbine) on a central shaft; breaks up air bubbles to increase gas-liquid contact area; prevents concentration gradients of nutrients and products; (3) Baffles — four vertical plates equally spaced on the inner wall; convert rotational flow into axial flow, improving mixing without increasing the energy input; (4) Sparger — porous ring at the bottom through which sterile compressed air or oxygen is introduced; smaller bubble size from finer pores gives higher oxygen transfer rate; (5) Jacket/cooling coils — water or refrigerant circulates to remove the heat of fermentation (exothermic) and maintain set temperature; (6) pH electrode — glass electrode measuring H+ ion activity; feedback controller adjusts acid (H2SO4) or base (NaOH) addition pumps to maintain set point; (7) Dissolved oxygen (DO) electrode — Clark polarographic membrane electrode; feedback control increases agitation speed or airflow rate when DO falls below set point; (8) Temperature probe — RTD or thermocouple; controls jacket water flow; (9) Foam detector — capacitance or optical probe; triggers antifoam pump to add silicone oil or polypropylene glycol; (10) Exhaust gas outlet — with sterile hydrophobic filter to prevent contamination via the gas phase; (11) Inoculation port and sampling port for aseptic operations.

Organism: Penicillium chrysogenum (also classified as P. rubens); a filamentous fungus; modern industrial strains have been selected by repeated mutagenesis for yields of >40,000 units/mL.
Medium: corn steep liquor (nitrogen, growth factors), lactose or slow-feed glucose (carbon source; fast glucose causes catabolite repression of penicillin biosynthesis), phenylacetic acid or sodium phenylacetate as side-chain precursor for Pen G, mineral salts.
Process conditions: fed-batch aerobic submerged fermentation; temperature 25–26°C; pH 6.0–6.5 (critical — penicillin is labile at extremes); dissolved oxygen > 30% air saturation; glucose fed slowly to avoid repression; precursor fed continuously to direct biosynthesis toward Pen G. Duration: 6–8 days.
Kinetics: penicillin is a secondary (non-growth-associated) metabolite produced in the idiophase (stationary phase) after active growth slows.
Extraction: (a) Mycelium removed by vacuum drum filter or centrifugation. (b) Broth acidified to pH 2–2.5 → penicillin is in its protonated (un-ionised) form and partitions into organic solvent (amyl acetate or butyl acetate; partition coefficient ~50). (c) Re-extracted into aqueous phosphate buffer pH 7 (back-extraction). (d) Activated charcoal treatment to remove colour. (e) Crystallisation as potassium penicillin G salt. The product undergoes sterility testing, LAL endotoxin test, HPLC purity, and bioassay before release.

questions.answer:
Industrial enzymes are produced mainly by submerged aerobic fermentation of bacteria or fungi, then purified and formulated.
General process: an inoculum of the enzyme-producing microorganism is prepared from a master cell bank; production fermentation is carried out in a stirred-tank bioreactor under controlled temperature, pH and DO; enzyme activity is monitored in samples; at peak activity the broth is harvested.
For extracellular enzymes (secreted by the organism, easier to recover): the cells are removed by centrifugation or filtration; the supernatant is concentrated by ultrafiltration; the enzyme is stabilised with preservatives or spray-dried.
For intracellular enzymes: cells are disrupted before recovery.
Three important industrial enzymes:
1. Alpha-amylase: produced by Bacillus licheniformis (high temperature stability) or Aspergillus oryzae; catalyses hydrolysis of alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch to dextrins and maltose; uses: starch processing for glucose syrup and high-fructose corn syrup production, baking (improves bread shelf life), textile desizing, detergents (for starch removal from fabrics and utensils).
2. Alkaline protease: produced by Bacillus subtilis, B. licheniformis, Aspergillus niger; hydrolyses peptide bonds at alkaline pH; uses: detergents (Subtilisin Carlsberg/Novo — the original detergent enzyme), leather processing (dehairing), food (meat tenderising), pharmaceutical (wound debridement).
3. Lipase: produced by Candida rugosa, Rhizomucor miehei, Thermomyces lanuginosus; hydrolyses ester bonds in triglycerides; uses: biodiesel production (transesterification of vegetable oils), fat removal in detergents, food processing (cheese flavour development), cosmetics.

questions.answer:
The Luedeking-Piret model describes the relationship between product formation and cell growth:
dP/dt = α (dX/dt) + β X
where P = product concentration, X = biomass concentration, α = growth-associated product formation coefficient (product formed per unit of new growth), β = non-growth-associated product formation coefficient (product formed per unit of biomass per unit time).
This model classifies products into three types:
1. Growth-associated (α >> 0, β ≈ 0): product formed in proportion to growth; e.g. primary metabolites such as ethanol by yeast, lactic acid by Lactobacillus. These are produced mainly during exponential phase.
2. Non-growth-associated (α ≈ 0, β >> 0): product formed in proportion to existing biomass, mainly during stationary phase (the idiophase); e.g. penicillin, streptomycin, erythromycin.
3. Mixed (both α and β significant): e.g. xanthan gum, amino acids under certain conditions.
Application to penicillin: penicillin biosynthesis begins in earnest only when growth slows (the idiophase), after nitrogen or phosphorus exhaustion triggers secondary metabolism. During rapid growth, intracellular cAMP is low and catabolite repression inhibits the biosynthesis genes pcbAB, pcbC and penDE. Fed-batch glucose feeding at low concentrations in the production fermenter keeps growth rate controlled and low, ensuring the cells remain in the idiophase for most of the fermentation and maximising the duration of non-growth-associated penicillin production.
questions.question: Explain the Luedeking-Piret model for secondary metabolite production. How does this apply to penicillin fermentation?

questions.answer:
Submerged fermentation (SmF): the microorganism is suspended in a liquid medium; most pharmaceutical fermentations use SmF. Conditions are well controlled (pH, DO, temperature); scale-up is straightforward; product quality is consistent; product is in the liquid phase and is easier to harvest. Disadvantages: large volumes of water and energy for aeration; wastewater treatment required. Examples: penicillin, streptomycin, erythromycin, glutamic acid, recombinant proteins, industrial enzymes (amylase, protease).
Solid-state fermentation (SSF): the microorganism grows on the surface of or within a moistened solid substrate at low water activity (20–70% moisture). No free water. The substrate is usually an agricultural residue (wheat bran, rice husk, sugarcane bagasse). Conditions are harder to control (heat and mass transfer limited; no good pH/DO control). Advantages: low water use, cheap substrates, high product concentration per gram of substrate, lower energy cost, traditional SSF is GRAS (generally recognised as safe). Disadvantages: difficult to scale, high heat generation, risk of contamination with complex non-sterile substrates, product extraction can be difficult. Examples: traditional Asian fermented foods (soy sauce via Aspergillus oryzae koji mould on steamed rice and soybean; tempeh via Rhizopus oligosporus on cooked soybean; miso); industrial enzyme production in developing countries (cellulase and xylanase by Trichoderma reesei on wheat bran); composting (SSF on a massive scale).
